elements.text: Management and maintenance personnel allowed the airplane to be released for flight with a known and unresolved discrepancy
Pilots decided to operate the airplane with a known discrepancy
The known discrepancy likely resulted in an in-flight fire
A weather radar system anomaly was documented the day before the accident
The anomaly was temporarily alleviated by pulling the circuit breaker without proper maintenance action
The airplane was flown without examining the weather radar system or following required regulatory procedures (placarding, records entry)
Pilots had sufficient information to determine the condition was a hazard but accepted the airplane anyway
No diagnostic, corrective, or interim maintenance action was taken to address the discrepancy
A pilot likely reset the weather radar circuit breaker, restoring power and causing the in-flight fire
Existing manufacturer guidance on resetting circuit breakers does not adequately address cumulative wiring damage
Lack of thorough understanding of hazards associated with resetting tripped circuit breakers among pilots and maintenance personnel
Lack of clear identification by manufacturers of which systems are critical to flight regarding circuit breaker resetting
Insufficient guidance and information for maintenance personnel regarding electrical system and wiring inspection best practices
Absence of a formal method to determine and ensure airplane airworthiness within the operator's standard operating procedures
The weather radar anomaly could have developed into a significant smoke and fire event
Insufficient evidence to determine the origin of the in-flight fire
It was not possible to determine the events leading to the airplane's maneuvers away from the airport
Safety Management System programs would provide a formal system of risk management and oversight
